name: Accuracy
seoDesc: Accuracy: work out false positive from the true positive and the accuracy. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the true positive, the accuracy, the prevalence and the sensitivity and the Accuracy calculator solves for false positive. It suits an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Accuracy calculator work?
sections.html:
The Accuracy calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports false positive in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select a method); then you type in the true positive, the accuracy, the prevalence and the sensitivity (2).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Accuracy calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

False positive=(-accuracy × (false negative + true negative + true positive) + true negative + true positive) ÷ accuracy
Accuracy=prevalence × sensitivity − prevalence × specificity + specificity
Sensitivity=true positive ÷ (false negative + true positive)
Specificity=true negative ÷ (false positive + true negative)
False negative=-true positive + true positive ÷ sensitivity
False positive=-true negative + true negative ÷ specificity

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Select a method set to Standard method, True positive = 10, False negative = 10 and True negative = 10. Working through the relationship above gives False positive = 170, Sensitivity = 50 % and Specificity = 5.5556 %.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: False positive = 170, Sensitivity = 50 % and Specificity = 5.5556 % should be roughly the size you expected from Select a method set to Standard method and True positive = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Accuracy calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the true positive, the accuracy and the prevalence — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Accuracy calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns false positive, derived from the true positive, the accuracy and the prevalence. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Accuracy calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the true positive, the accuracy, the prevalence and the sensitivity, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter accuracy in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Accuracy opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports False positive = 170. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Accuracy calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
